rationale: Matthew 7:26 directly identifies the foolish man as one who hears Christ’s sayings and does not do them, while the surrounding contrast identifies the obedient hearer as wise. Psalm 14:1 associates the fool with practical godlessness, corruption, and evil works rather than deficient intelligence. The common interpretation is broader, but it does not contradict the entry’s core referent: refusing to obey God’s word is a concrete form of moral-spiritual rebellion. Although the evidence does not prove that every biblical use of “fool” requires an explicitly narrated act of hearing, no supplied text contradicts the entry, and the exact hearing-versus-doing formulation best explains Matthew’s wise/foolish contrast.
book_core_identification: A fool is a person who hears God’s word but refuses to obey it.
book_secondary_elaborations: The fool is the opposite of the wise.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s identification of the ten virgins with the ten-tribe house of Israel depends on a disputed textual reading and an extended typological chain not required by the glossary entry.
The claim that the virgins’ oil specifically means Spirit-taught correction and proven obedience is substantially more contestable than the glossary definition.
The chapter’s uniform-symbol method may understate contextual and lexical variation among the several biblical words translated “fool.”
The proposed symbolic connections involving Gethsemane, the Mount of Olives, Israel as the olive nation, and pressed oil are chapter-level typology rather than support necessary for the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The biblical fool is more broadly a morally and spiritually rebellious person who rejects God, divine wisdom, or correction and lives by self-directed judgment; hearing God’s word and failing to do it is one manifestation of this broader folly, not its exhaustive definition.
counter_core_identification: A fool is a morally and spiritually rebellious or practically godless person, whether or not a passage explicitly portrays that person as first hearing God’s word.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that explicit prior hearing followed by nonperformance is a necessary or exhaustive defining condition of every biblical fool.
counter_case: Psalm 14:1 directly emphasizes practical denial of God, corruption, and abominable works without expressly stating that the fool has heard God’s word.
Matthew 7:26 can be read as applying the already familiar category of folly to a disobedient hearer rather than defining every occurrence of the category.
Proverbs describes fools through several overlapping traits—despising instruction, self-trust, resistance to correction, and wrongdoing—supporting a broader moral-spiritual category.
book_explanatory_advantages: Matthew 7:26 states the entry’s hearing-and-not-doing identification almost verbatim.
The wise/foolish opposition is explicit in Matthew 7:24–27: both hear, but only the wise person does.
Psalm 14:1 links folly to corrupt conduct, supporting the entry’s rejection of an intelligence-based meaning.
The entry gives a concrete behavioral criterion that unifies practical godlessness with disobedience rather than leaving folly as an undefined moral label.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The broader interpretation accommodates biblical passages where folly is described without an explicit hearing event.
It better preserves the lexical and contextual range of “fool” across Psalms, Proverbs, parables, and Pauline ironic usage.
It treats nonobedience in Matthew 7 as a particularly clear instance of moral-spiritual folly rather than necessarily an exhaustive lexical definition.
unresolved_objections: Psalm 14:1 does not itself mention the fool hearing God’s word, so the entry’s exact formulation relies chiefly on Matthew 7.
The word “lawless” is a reasonable theological summary of deliberate nonobedience, but it is not the exact vocabulary of either printed reference.
The entry is narrower than the full range of biblical usages, especially ironic expressions such as “fools for Christ,” though those distinct usages do not defeat its stated core referent.
